hook: Claude Sonnet 5.5 and GPT-6.1 Sol list the same price: $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output. The same thousand documents do not cost the same on both, because one tokenizer counts about 30% more tokens for the same text.

sections.title: Two sheets, one identical sticker
sections.content:
The flagship rows of both price sheets match to the cent, and so do the cache reads.

| Per million tokens | Claude Sonnet 5.5 | GPT-6.1 Sol |
|---|---|---|
| Input | $2.00 | $2.00 |
| Output | $10.00 | $10.00 |
| Cached input (hit) | $0.10 | $0.10 |
| 5m or 30m cache write | $2.50 (1.25x) | $2.50 (1.25x) |
| Batch input / output | $1.00 / $5.00 | $1.00 / $5.00 |

Anthropic's Opus 5.5 sits one rung up at $4 and $20, with cache reads at $0.20. OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra sits at $10 and $50. On the flagship row there is nothing to choose, which is the first sign that the model price is not the decision.

sections.title: The tokenizer changes the invoice before your prompt does
sections.content:
Anthropic's pricing page carries a note most price sheets would leave out: Claude 4.7 and later use a newer tokenizer that produces approximately 30% more tokens for the same text.

So the sticker is $2 per million tokens, and the bill is $2 per million tokens of Claude's counting. For text that costs $2.00 per million source tokens on a standard tokenizer, the same text costs $2.00 × 1.3 = $2.60.

That is a 30% difference on the largest line of a RAG or agent bill, and it does not appear anywhere in a side-by-side table that compares per-token prices. The note also says the exact increase depends on the content, so treat 1.3 as a working multiplier, not a constant.

sections.title: Caching is a break-even test, not a discount
sections.content:
Both vendors sell the same shape: pay more to write a prefix, pay less to read it. The multipliers are where they part.

| Cache operation | Anthropic | OpenAI |
|---|---|---|
| Write, short | 1.25x, 5 minutes | 1.25x, 30 minutes |
| Write, long | 2x, 1 hour | 2.5x, 12 hours |
| Read (hit) | 0.1x, or 0.05x on 5.5 models | 0.05x |

A cached prefix costs 1.25 + 0.1n to serve n requests, against n uncached. The break-even is n = 1.39, so the second request already wins, and ten requests cost 2.25 instead of 10, a 77.5% cut on the input line. The long windows are worse deals for short runs: 2x + 0.1n beats n only from the third request, and OpenAI's 2.5x write needs three reads before it pays.

sections.title: Batch is the one line where both sheets agree
sections.content:
Both vendors halve input and output for asynchronous work. Anthropic publishes the batch rows separately; OpenAI prints a Batch table and a separate Flex table at the same numbers.

| Batch, per million | Claude Sonnet 5.5 | Claude Opus 5.5 | GPT-6.1 Sol |
|---|---|---|---|
| Input | $1.00 | $2.00 | $1.00 |
| Output | $5.00 | $10.00 | $5.00 |

Anthropic's page says its cache multipliers stack with the batch discount. That combination is the cheapest published way to process a large, stable corpus: a cached prefix at 0.1x inside a batch, on a job that can wait. The trap is that a nightly single-run job has nothing to read from, and a cold cache write just adds 25% to a batch you could have submitted uncached.

sections.title: Long prompts are where the sheets stop being comparable
sections.content:
Both vendors reprice the prompt once it gets long, and they do it in different shapes.

| Prompt size | GPT-6.1 Sol | Claude Haiku 5.5 |
|---|---|---|
| Short context, input | $2.00 | $0.10 up to 100,000 tokens |
| Long context, input | $4.00 | $0.50 over 100,000 tokens |
| Long context, output | $15.00 | $2.50 over 100,000 tokens |

OpenAI's long-context row doubles input and multiplies output by 1.5. Anthropic's Haiku sheet lists two rows, one for prompts up to 100,000 tokens and one for prompts over it, at five times the rate, and it does not print a marginal split.

A 200,000-token prompt therefore bills at 0.2 × $0.50 = $0.10 on the over-100k row against $0.02 if the same prompt fit under the line. That cliff, not the per-token sticker, is what a document pipeline hits when someone pastes a whole contract set.

sections.title: Three add-ons that quietly change the unit
sections.content:
Fast mode on both sides doubles the sticker: Opus 5.5 goes to $8 input and $40 output, GPT-6.1 Sol to $4 and $20. Anthropic notes that fast mode is not available with the Batch API, so the two savings cannot be stacked.

Data residency is a multiplier rather than a tier. Sending Claude 4.6 or later to US-only inference applies 1.1x to every token category, cache writes and reads included.

The third is the cache window, and it is easy to lose money on. A 12-hour write costs 2.5x, so a job that runs twice a day should skip caching entirely rather than pay 2.5x for a prefix it reads once. Check the read count before enabling it: three reads is where the long window starts to earn.

cost_math.label: 100k requests, 16k cached prefix, 4k fresh input, 500 output
cost_math.result: $1,844 on either vendor at list price, before the tokenizer

cost_math.label: The same workload through a tokenizer that counts 30% more
cost_math.result: $2,397 against $1,844 for identical text, a 30% difference on a sheet whose per-token prices match

cost_math.label: Cache break-even on a shared prefix
cost_math.formula: 1.25 + 0.10n < n, so n > 1.39; at n = 10 the cost is 1.25 + 1.00 = 2.25 against 10 uncached
cost_math.result: Profitable from the second request; 77.5% off the input line by the tenth

cost_math.label: Long window write on a twice-daily job
cost_math.formula: OpenAI 12h: 2.5 write + 0.10 read = 2.60, against 2 × 1.00 = 2.00 uncached. Anthropic 1h: 2.0 write + 0.10 read = 2.10, against 2.00
cost_math.result: 2.6 against 2.0: caching a prefix read twice costs more than not caching it under either vendor's long window

decision_matrix.situation: A long, stable system prompt at high volume
decision_matrix.why: Both bill the prefix at 1.25x to write and 0.10x or 0.05x to read, so a 30% token difference decides more than the cache terms do.
OpenAI doubles input and multiplies output by 1.5 past the boundary; Haiku 5.5 lists a rate five times higher for prompts over 100,000 tokens.

decision_matrix.situation: Nightly batch of a few hundred thousand jobs
decision_matrix.why: Both halve input and output, and a single nightly pass has no cache to read from, so a cold write only adds 25%.

decision_matrix.situation: A job that runs every 12 hours over one corpus
decision_matrix.why: The 12-hour write costs 2.5x and the 1-hour write has expired by the next run; two uncached passes cost 2.0 against 2.6.
Output is 5x input on both sheets, so the $10 against $20 output rate dominates the bill long before the input line does.

decision_matrix.situation: Streaming that a user is watching
decision_matrix.why: Opus 5.5 moves to $8 and $40 and GPT-6.1 Sol to $4 and $20, and fast mode cannot be combined with batch.

decision_matrix.situation: Data must stay in the US
decision_matrix.why: US-only inference multiplies every Claude token category by 1.1, cache writes and reads included, which changes a close comparison.

decision_matrix.situation: A prototype with prompts under 100,000 tokens
decision_matrix.why: $0.10 input and $0.50 output per million is a twentieth of the flagship rows, and the over-100k rate only applies when the prompt crosses the line.

verdict_summary: On the flagship row the two sheets are the same page: $2 in, $10 out, $0.10 cached. The choice is decided by three things that are not on that row, the tokenizer's 30% count, the long-context shape, and how many times your prefix is actually read. If your prompts stay under 100,000 tokens and your cache is warm, you are choosing a vendor on arithmetic that differs by a few percent; if they cross the line, you are choosing on a cliff.
migration_guide:
Moving between the two APIs is mostly a prompt rewrite, because the cache is the part that does not travel: Anthropic takes an explicit breakpoint marker, OpenAI caches a stable prefix automatically. Re-measure your token counts on the new tokenizer before you migrate pricing assumptions, since the same text will not bill the same number of tokens.

Everything asynchronous needs resubmission. Batch jobs, files and fine-tuned endpoints are per-vendor objects with no portable format, and model deprecations retire a SKU you may still be calling, so keep the model name in configuration rather than in code.

faqs.q: Is prompt caching automatic on both?
faqs.a: No. Anthropic takes a cache_control marker on the block you want cached, and OpenAI caches a stable prefix automatically with no marker to place.

faqs.q: Do the batch discount and the cache discount combine?
faqs.a: On Anthropic the page says cache multipliers stack with the batch discount. OpenAI publishes separate Batch and Flex tables at the same rates, and fast mode is excluded from batch on Anthropic.

faqs.q: What does the 30% tokenizer note change?
faqs.a: It raises the effective price per unit of source text by about 30% on Claude 4.7 and later, against a sheet whose per-token rates are otherwise identical to the competitor's.

faqs.q: Is a cache write ever a loss?
faqs.a: Yes. The 1.25x short write needs a read to pay for itself and the 2x or 2.5x long write needs two or three, so a job that reads the prefix once bills more with caching than without.
